one_liner: Radford Neal's fork of GNU R 2.15 with a faster interpreter, GC and builtins; beats R-3.4/3.5 on many operations.
what_it_does: pqR is a complete R interpreter and distribution (base, recommended packages, Fortran/C numerics) derived from R-2.15.0 and versioned as 2.15.1, with selected features and bug fixes back-ported from R Core releases up to about R-3.5. You run R scripts with it instead of GNU R; it is source-compatible with R-2.15-era code, but compiled packages must be reinstalled against it and packages that need R 3.x or 4.x often do not install. It also adds language extensions (for ... down/across, !! and ! as paste operators, list arithmetic, preliminary automatic differentiation).
how_it_is_fast: The speed comes from many interpreter-level changes rather than a JIT: a 3-bit NAMEDCNT reference count that avoids needless duplication, unmaterialized integer sequences (for (i in 1:n) and x[101:200] allocate no index vector), in-place vector growth and subassignment, 'static boxes' and a scalar stack for scalar results, and fused operations such as sum(vec>0) without the intermediate. A deferred-evaluation framework does 'task merging' (exp(v+1) in one loop) and runs long vector operations in OpenMP 'helper threads' with pipelining between tasks. Memory uses the Segmented Generational Garbage Collector (radfordneal/sggc) with optional 32-bit compressed pointers. Builtins were rewritten piecemeal: a recursive-descent parser, hashed sample(), faster paste/substr/number-to-string conversion, serialize without Sun XDR, data.table's radix sort plus a merge sort, and a SIMD matrix multiply (matprod) that keeps naive summation order.
when_to_use: Legacy R-2.15-era scripts dominated by vector or list subassignment (x[a:b] <- v, l$x <- v), paste/paste0, number-string conversion, sample() of few items from a large set, or sort/order, where the release notes and author timings show several-fold gains over R-3.4/3.5.
Machines with spare cores running long-vector arithmetic: helper threads (pqR --helpers N) parallelize and pipeline elementwise math and matrix products with no code changes.
Work that needs bit-reproducible floating point: pqR forces -ffp-contract=off, checks for fused multiply-add at startup and its matrix products reproduce naive sequential summation.
Studying how to speed up an R-style interpreter: NEWS, MODS and the R Internals manual document each optimization.
when_not_to_use: Any project that needs current R: NEWS back-ports items only up to about R-3.5, so R 4.x features (for example the native |> pipe) are absent, and CRAN packages requiring R >= 3.x usually fail to install or need DESCRIPTION edits.

Scalar-loop-heavy code: GitHub issue #49 (2021) times while/repeat loops decrementing a counter 1e6 times at about 97 ms in pqR 2.15.1 versus about 41/36 ms in GNU R 4.0.3, so modern R with its default byte-compiler JIT is about 2.4x faster there.

Production use: abandoned since 2020-07-23, with open crash reports (#43 buffer overflow with attributes on a recursive function, #44 floating point exception, #45 abort in plot) and open build failures on Ubuntu 20.04 (#46) and Slackware 15.0 (#48).
BLAS-bound linear algebra: the built-in matprod routines are by NEWS's own account up to about 2x slower than OpenBLAS (an external BLAS can be linked, losing the reproducibility guarantee).
Windows or RStudio-centric setups: no Windows binary (issue #34), RStudio needs --enable-R-shlib, and a Mac GUI issue with helper threads (#17) is open.

integration.form: Full interpreter built from source (configure && make); optional shared libR with --enable-R-shlib
integration.dependencies: C, C++ and Fortran compilers (gcc/gfortran per INSTALL), OpenMP 3.0/3.1 for helper threads, system zlib, bzip2, pcre and xz/liblzma dev packages; optional external BLAS/LAPACK
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (INSTALL suggests CC='gcc -std=gnu99') plus gfortran; the 2020-07-23 release adds fixes for gcc-10 and recent gfortran; newer toolchains not documented
integration.platforms: Linux and other Unix including macOS and Solaris (INSTALL); Windows only by building from src/gnuwin32; requires correct 64-bit IEEE double (no x87-only Pentium III or earlier)
integration.thread_safety: R code runs in one interpreter thread; helper threads parallelize internal vector tasks; an external BLAS is assumed not thread-safe unless configured with BLAS_in_helpers=TRUE
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — source-compatible with R-2.15.1 scripts, but compiled packages must be reinstalled and most packages built for R 3.x/4.x are not supported

gotchas: The byte compiler is off by default and the JIT can never be enabled; byte-compiled code bypasses task merging, helper threads and unmaterialized sequences, so forcing it (R_USE_BYTECODE=TRUE) usually slows pqR down.

--enable-compressed-pointers saves memory but slows the interpreter by up to about 40% (INSTALL; NEWS says up to about 30%), and packages with C code must be built with the same compressed-pointer and aux-for-attrib settings as the interpreter.

Behaviour differs from GNU R in places: necessary parentheses are dropped from parsed expressions (breaks formula-sensitive packages such as coxme), else at the start of a top-level line is accepted, and the interpreter aborts on a PROTECT stack imbalance that GNU R only warns about.
The headline gains are microbenchmarks of single operations; the author's 17x figure times one statement (a[2:19999] <- 3.1) that exercises pqR's no-index-vector range subscript path.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only R implementation catalogued; unlike PyPy, TruffleRuby or LuaJIT it is an evolved fork of the reference interpreter with no JIT, so choose it only to run R-2.15-compatible code faster where vector and string builtins dominate, not as a general accelerator for modern R.
verified_claims_summary: All numbers are first-party: NEWS says paste/paste0 are 2-6x faster than R-3.4.0 and the parser about 1.5x faster than R-3.2.2, and the author's 2018-11-25 blog (WebSearch snippet only, blog blocked here) times a[2:19999] <- 3.1 run 100,000 times at 0.257 s versus 4.360 s in R-3.5.1, both built with gcc 8.2.0 -O3 on an Intel Skylake. No benchmark scripts are in the repo; the only third-party timing found (issue #49) shows GNU R 4.0.3 about 2.4x faster than pqR on simple scalar loops.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2020-07-23, 21 open issues including an unanswered 2024 'Status of the project?' (#50); GPL-2 or GPL-3, usable for running legacy R-2.15-era code or as a reference for interpreter optimizations, not as a current R replacement.
